title: Culture: How Everyday Norms Shape the Work
outcomes: Name three unwritten norms in their own team.
Tell the difference between a standard and a habit of perfectionism.
Respond to a mistake, theirs or someone else's, in a way that keeps learning open.
summary: Every team has habits nobody wrote down. This course helps staff notice the everyday norms that shape how work gets done, and see when a norm helps the people we serve and when it gets in the way.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Culture: How Everyday Norms Shape the Work
The habits nobody wrote down
Foundation self-directed learning

Opening case

The new colleague, three months in, sends a client letter with one typo. Within an hour it is mentioned in a team chat, a reply-all and a one-on-one. Nobody is unkind. The new colleague stops sending anything without three people checking it.

What culture means here

Culture is what people do when the policy is silent. It shows in who speaks first, what gets praised and what gets quietly corrected. You learn it by watching, long before anyone explains it.

Norms are not good or bad by themselves

Double-checking a benefits letter protects a family. Double-checking every email slows the team and teaches people to fear small errors. The same habit can help in one place and harm in another.

Where norms come from

Most norms started as a fix for a real problem. Over time the problem fades and the habit stays. Asking where a norm came from is often the fastest way to see whether it still fits.

Standards and perfectionism

A standard says what good work looks like. Perfectionism treats any flaw as a sign of failure. The first helps people improve. The second teaches people to hide mistakes.

How defensiveness shows up

When a concern is raised, the first reaction is often to explain why it isn't a problem. That is human. When it becomes the team's habit, people stop raising concerns.

What it costs the people we serve

When staff fear mistakes, they slow down, hold decisions and avoid asking for help. The family waiting on an answer feels that delay, even if they never see the cause.

Practice: a habit of extra checking
The case manager notices the new colleague has started asking three people to review every routine email. What does the case manager do?
A. Says nothing, since extra checking can't hurt.
B. Tells the new colleague, "You don't need to run everything by us. Routine emails are fine to send."
C. Asks the new colleague what prompted the extra checks, then shares which messages truly need a second look.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Noticing your team's norms

Three questions help: What happens when someone makes a mistake? Who gets credit, and for what? What would a new person be afraid to ask?

Mistakes as information

A mistake tells you something about the process, not just the person. Asking what made the error easy to make leads to better fixes than asking who made it.

Practice: an error in a notice
A client's appointment notice went out with the wrong office address. In the team meeting, what does the supervisor ask first?
A. "Who sent this?"
B. "What in our process made this easy to miss?"
C. "Let's just be more careful."
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Raising a concern without blame

Describe what you saw, say why it matters and ask a question. For example: "I noticed the letter went out with the old date. Can we look at how that step works?"

Receiving a concern

Thank the person, ask one question before you explain and decide what you will change. You can disagree later, after you understand.

Practice: a concern from a partner
The county partner tells the program manager that families say the team's letters are hard to understand. The program manager's first response?
A. Explains that the letters follow the required template.
B. Thanks the county partner and asks which parts families struggle with.
C. Promises to rewrite every letter.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Small moves that shift a norm

Saying "I got that wrong" in a meeting. Thanking someone for catching your error. Asking a new colleague what surprised them. Norms change through repeated small acts.

What this is not

This is not about lowering standards or ignoring errors that harm people. It is about fixing errors in a way that keeps people willing to speak up.

Rewrite activity

Rewrite this message so it fixes the error and keeps learning open: "This is the second time this week. Please be more careful." (A suggested rewrite appears after the learner submits.)

Your team's next step

Pick one norm you noticed today. Write one sentence on whether it still serves the people your team supports.

Shared culture, real responsibilities

Culture belongs to everyone, and supervisors carry more of it. What a supervisor praises, corrects or ignores teaches the whole team.

Reflection

What is one norm you would keep, and one you would question?

Closing

Norms are learned, so they can be relearned. Noticing them is where it starts.

practice.title: Practice: a habit of extra checking
practice.question: The case manager notices the new colleague has started asking three people to review every routine email. What does the case manager do?

options.text: Says nothing, since extra checking can't hurt.
options.feedback: Extra checking has a cost. The new colleague's work slows, and the habit of fear goes unnamed.

options.text: Tells the new colleague, "You don't need to run everything by us. Routine emails are fine to send."
options.feedback: Helpful, and clear. It may not reach the reason the new colleague started checking.

options.text: Asks the new colleague what prompted the extra checks, then shares which messages truly need a second look.
options.feedback: This names the norm, finds where it came from and gives the new colleague a clear line between a standard and a fear.

practice.question: A client's appointment notice went out with the wrong office address. In the team meeting, what does the supervisor ask first?

options.text: "Who sent this?"
options.feedback: It finds the person, but not the step that made the error easy.

options.text: "What in our process made this easy to miss?"
options.feedback: This treats the error as information and points the team at a fix that protects the next client.

options.text: "Let's just be more careful."
options.feedback: It sounds reasonable, but it changes nothing and adds pressure.

options.feedback: Well meant, but it commits before understanding the problem.

title: Pace, Pressure and Decision Quality
audience: Staff who lead work, supervisors and team leads
outcomes: Sort a week's urgent requests into true deadlines and habits of urgency.
Name what gets lost when a team counts output over outcomes.
Use a short pause routine before a decision that affects a client or community.
summary: Public service runs on deadlines, and some of them are real. This course helps people tell a true deadline from a habit of urgency, and protect the quality of decisions that affect people's lives when the pressure is on.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Pace, Pressure and Decision Quality
When everything is urgent
Intermediate self-directed learning

Opening case

The program manager's division is asked to roll out a new eligibility process in two weeks. The team hits the date. A month later, the county partner reports that families who speak Somali never got the notice in their language.

Real deadlines and urgency as a habit

Some deadlines come from law, funding or a person in crisis. Others come from habit. Both feel the same in the moment, which is why the difference is worth checking.

What urgency costs

Rushing cuts the steps that are easiest to skip: checking with partners, testing with the people affected and translating. Those are often the steps that protect access.

Quantity over quality

Teams measure what is easy to count, such as cases closed, emails answered or trainings held. When the count becomes the goal, the outcome for the person can drop out of view.

Who pays for speed

The people with the least power to push back often absorb the cost of a rushed decision. That includes clients with limited English, people with disabilities and frontline staff.

Asking where the date came from

A simple question, "What happens if this lands a week later?", often shows whether a deadline is fixed or chosen.

Practice: an end-of-day request
The supervisor gets a request at 4 p.m. to send updated guidance to all case managers by end of day. What do they do first?
A. Sends it out as is.
B. Asks the sender what happens if it goes out at 10 a.m. tomorrow.
C. Stays late to rewrite it fully.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

The pause routine

Before a decision that affects people, ask three things: Who is affected? Who haven't we heard from? What would we do differently with one more day?

Using the pause under pressure

The pause can take ten minutes. It doesn't stop the work. It makes sure the work reaches everyone it should.

Measuring what matters

Pair every count with one question about the outcome. For example: cases closed, and how many clients understood their next step.

Practice: a record month
The division's monthly report shows 400 cases closed, a record. What does the program manager ask?
A. "Can we hit 450 next month?"
B. "How many of those families came back within 30 days?"
C. "Great work, everyone."
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Pushing back on a deadline

Name the risk, offer a choice and propose a date. "We can launch on the 1st in English, or on the 8th in all four languages. Which do you want?"

When the deadline is real

Sometimes there is no extra week. Then the job is to name what was cut, tell the people affected and plan when to come back to it.

Practice: a deadline set by law
The launch date is set by law and can't move. Translation won't be ready. What does the program manager do?
A. Launches and says nothing about the gap.
B. Launches, tells county partners which languages are late and sets a date for the rest.
C. Delays the launch anyway.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Supervisors set the pace

When a supervisor treats every request as urgent, the team learns that everything is. Marking what can wait is a leadership act.

What this is not

This is not permission to miss deadlines that matter. It is a way to spend urgency where it belongs.

Rewrite activity

Rewrite this request so it states the real deadline and what matters most: "Need this ASAP, drop everything."

Your team's next step

List this week's three most urgent requests. Mark each one as fixed or chosen.

Shared culture, real responsibilities

Everyone can ask where a date came from. Supervisors and managers decide which dates move, so they carry the larger share of the pace.

Reflection

When did speed last cost someone access, and what would have caught it?

Closing

The work is urgent because people are waiting. That is the reason to get it right for all of them.

options.feedback: One question shows whether the deadline is fixed, and buys time to check the guidance if it isn't.

options.feedback: Dedicated, and it may not be needed. Pace set this way is hard to sustain.

options.feedback: It rewards the count, and the count may already hide a problem.

options.feedback: This pairs the count with an outcome and shows whether closing fast meant closing well.

options.feedback: Recognition matters, and it is stronger when it is tied to outcomes.

title: Building a Learning Organization
outcomes: Map how information about problems reaches them today.
Run a blameless review of a decision that went wrong.
Share one decision with the people it affects before it is final.
summary: Leaders shape culture through the systems they build: how decisions are made, who hears about problems and what gets reviewed after something goes wrong. This course helps leaders design routines that let a division learn from its own work, including from the people closest to the community.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Building a Learning Organization
Leading so the whole division can learn
Advanced self-directed learning

Opening case

A policy change the program manager's director approved has caused confusion for months. Frontline staff knew in week one. The news reached the director in month four, in a complaint from a legislator's office.

What a learning organization is

A learning organization notices what isn't working and changes, without waiting for a crisis. It depends less on smart individuals and more on routines that move what people know to where decisions are made.

Culture is built by systems

Leaders teach culture through what they pay attention to, how they react to bad news and who they promote. Those signals outweigh any values statement.

Power and information

When decisions sit with a few people, so does information. Staff stop sharing what leaders can't act on, and leaders decide with half the picture.

The written word and other ways of knowing

A memo is not the only form of evidence. What a case manager hears at a kitchen table, or what a county partner sees in the waiting room, is data too.

Either/or thinking

"Either we follow the policy or we make exceptions" hides the third option: learn why the policy isn't working and fix it.

Practice: staff who "resist" a process
In a leadership meeting, someone says frontline staff are "resisting" the new intake process. What does the director say?
A. "Remind them it's required."
B. "What are they seeing that we aren't?"
C. "Let's give it more time."
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Mapping how bad news travels

Draw how a problem on the front line reaches you. Count the steps. Each step is a place where the message can soften, stall or stop.

Blameless review

After something goes wrong, ask what happened, what made sense to people at the time and what the system made easy or hard. Leave out who to blame. People tell the truth when it is safe to.

Running the review

Invite the people who did the work, including partners. Set the ground rules aloud. End with two or three changes and an owner for each.

Practice: a review that turns to blame
In a blameless review, a supervisor starts to say which case manager made the error. What does the facilitator do?
A. Lets them finish.
B. Gently redirects: "Let's stay with what the process made easy or hard."
C. Ends the review.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Sharing decisions before they are final

Bring a draft to the people it affects. Ask what you missed. You keep the decision. You lose the surprises.

Feedback loops that last

A quarterly listening session with frontline staff. A standing agenda item for partner concerns. A rule that every new process gets a 60-day check.

Practice: a draft partners have not seen
The program manager has a draft policy ready to send. County partners haven't seen it. What does the program manager do?
A. Sends it and invites feedback afterward.
B. Shares the draft with the county partner's group for one week, with two questions.
C. Holds it until every partner agrees.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Your own reaction is the signal

The first time someone brings you bad news, your reaction tells them whether to do it again. Thank them before you respond to the content.

What this is not

A learning organization still makes decisions and holds people accountable. It just learns before it blames.

Rewrite activity

Rewrite this leadership update so it invites learning: "The new intake process is working as designed. Please follow it."

Your division's next step

Choose one recent decision. Plan a 45-minute blameless review with the people closest to it.

Shared culture, real responsibilities

Everyone can raise what they see. Leaders decide whether the system hears it, so the design of feedback loops is a leadership responsibility.

Reflection

What is something your division knows that you, as a leader, may not?

Closing

A division learns at the speed its leaders can hear bad news.

practice.title: Practice: staff who "resist" a process
practice.question: In a leadership meeting, someone says frontline staff are "resisting" the new intake process. What does the director say?

options.text: "Remind them it's required."
options.feedback: It restates the rule and misses the chance to learn why staff are struggling.

options.text: "What are they seeing that we aren't?"
options.feedback: This treats resistance as information and opens a path to fix the process.

options.text: "Let's give it more time."
options.feedback: Patience can help, and without a question attached it can also delay a needed fix.

practice.title: Practice: a review that turns to blame
practice.question: In a blameless review, a supervisor starts to say which case manager made the error. What does the facilitator do?

options.text: Lets them finish.
options.feedback: The room learns that this review is about blame after all.

options.text: Gently redirects: "Let's stay with what the process made easy or hard."
options.feedback: This keeps the ground rules and keeps people willing to speak.

options.text: Ends the review.
options.feedback: It avoids conflict and loses the learning.

practice.title: Practice: a draft partners have not seen
practice.question: The program manager has a draft policy ready to send. County partners haven't seen it. What does the program manager do?

options.text: Sends it and invites feedback afterward.
options.feedback: Feedback after a decision is final rarely changes it, and partners know that.

options.text: Shares the draft with the county partner's group for one week, with two questions.
options.feedback: A short, focused review catches problems early and builds trust.

options.text: Holds it until every partner agrees.
options.feedback: Consensus can stall urgent work. Sharing before deciding is not the same as needing agreement.

title: Well-Being at Work: Sustainable Pace and Meaningful Work
outcomes: Describe what a sustainable week looks like for them.
Name two early signs that their pace isn't working.
Find the support options their workplace offers and know how to ask for them.
summary: Work in human services matters, and it can wear people down. This course helps staff notice their own pace, protect the parts of the work that give it meaning and ask for support early, without treating well-being as one more thing to get right.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Well-Being at Work: Sustainable Pace and Meaningful Work
Doing work that matters without running on empty
Foundation self-directed learning

Opening case

The case manager has carried a full caseload for two years and is good at it. Lately the case manager answers email at 10 p.m., skips lunch and feels flat even after a good outcome for a family.

Why well-being belongs at work

How people feel at work shapes how they treat clients, colleagues and themselves. Well-being isn't a perk. It is part of doing the job well over time.

Well-being is shared

Personal habits matter, and so do workload, staffing and how a team runs. This course covers both, and never asks you to fix alone what the system needs to fix.

What sustainable pace means

A sustainable pace is one you could keep for a year. Some weeks will be heavier. The question is whether you recover between them.

Meaning as a source of energy

Most people came to this work for a reason. Remembering that reason, and noticing when the work still delivers it, is one of the strongest supports there is.

Early signs your pace isn't working

Short temper, trouble switching off, dreading tasks you used to like and feeling numb after good news. These are signals, not failures.

Practice: an evening email
It's 9:45 p.m. The case manager sees a non-urgent email from a colleague. What does the case manager do?
A. Answers it now so it's done.
B. Leaves it for the morning.
C. Schedules a reply to send at 8 a.m.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Small protections

A real lunch break. A fixed time you stop checking email. A five-minute pause after a hard call. Small protections add up.

Boundaries that serve clients too

A rested case manager catches more and listens better. Protecting your time is part of protecting the people you serve.

Asking for support early

It is easier to adjust a workload or a schedule before a crisis than after. Asking early is a skill, not a weakness.

Practice: a growing caseload
The case manager's caseload has grown by a third since spring. What does the case manager do?
A. Keeps going, since everyone is busy.
B. Raises it with the supervisor and brings the numbers.
C. Starts looking for another job without saying anything.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Supporting a colleague

Notice, ask and listen. "You've seemed stretched lately. How are you doing?" You don't need to fix it. You can point to support.

Where support lives

Your supervisor, the Employee Assistance Program and your agency's leave and flexibility options. Find out what your workplace offers before you need it.

Practice: a colleague who seems withdrawn
The new colleague notices the case manager seems withdrawn in meetings. What does the new colleague do?
A. Says nothing, since it isn't the new colleague's business.
B. Asks privately, "How are you doing? You've seemed stretched lately."
C. Mentions it to the whole team.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

When it's more than stress

If you are struggling to cope, or thinking about harming yourself, reach out now. In the U.S., you can call or text 988. You don't need to be in crisis to talk to someone.

What this is not

This course doesn't measure anyone's well-being or ask you to share anything personal. It offers ideas you can use as you choose.

Rewrite activity

Rewrite this out-of-office note so it sets a clear, kind boundary: "I'll try to check messages while I'm out."

Your next step

Pick one small protection to try for the next two weeks.

Shared culture, real responsibilities

Everyone can look out for each other. Supervisors and managers control workload and schedules, so they carry more of the responsibility for a sustainable pace.

Reflection

What part of your work still gives you energy, and how can you protect it?

Closing

Good work over the long run needs people who can keep doing it.

practice.question: It's 9:45 p.m. The case manager sees a non-urgent email from a colleague. What does the case manager do?

options.text: Answers it now so it's done.
options.feedback: It clears the inbox and teaches everyone, the case manager included, that evenings are work time.

options.text: Leaves it for the morning.
options.feedback: Nothing is lost, and the case manager gets real time off.

options.text: Schedules a reply to send at 8 a.m.
options.feedback: A good middle path. It keeps the work off the evening for others, too.

practice.title: Practice: a growing caseload
practice.question: The case manager's caseload has grown by a third since spring. What does the case manager do?

options.text: Keeps going, since everyone is busy.
options.feedback: Common, and the cost builds quietly until it shows up in the work or in the case manager's health.

options.text: Raises it with the supervisor and brings the numbers.
options.feedback: Asking early, with facts, gives the supervisor something to act on.

options.text: Starts looking for another job without saying anything.
options.feedback: That may be the case manager's right choice in the end, and the team never got the chance to fix the workload.

practice.title: Practice: a colleague who seems withdrawn
practice.question: The new colleague notices the case manager seems withdrawn in meetings. What does the new colleague do?

options.text: Says nothing, since it isn't the new colleague's business.
options.feedback: Respecting privacy matters, and a kind check-in doesn't invade it.

options.text: Asks privately, "How are you doing? You've seemed stretched lately."
options.feedback: Simple and caring. The case manager can share as much or as little as they want.

options.text: Mentions it to the whole team.
options.feedback: Well meant, and it puts the case manager on the spot.

title: Workload, Burnout and Team Practices That Help
audience: Supervisors, team leads and staff who coordinate work
outcomes: Name the common workplace drivers of burnout.
Run a workload conversation that leads to a real change.
Set up two team practices that protect recovery time.
summary: Burnout is mostly a work problem, not a personal one. This course helps people who shape a team's work spot the conditions that drive burnout and put in place team practices that spread the load fairly and give people room to recover.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Workload, Burnout and Team Practices That Help
Fixing the work, not just the worker
Intermediate self-directed learning

Opening case

The supervisor's team lost two positions last year and the work stayed the same. Two people are on leave. The ones left are covering, and the most reliable person, the case manager, is covering most.

What burnout is

Burnout is long-term exhaustion, growing distance from the work and a sense that effort doesn't make a difference. It comes from chronic work stress that hasn't been managed.

Burnout is a work condition

Research points to drivers such as workload, lack of control, too little recognition, unfairness and values that clash with the job. Most of them sit with how work is organized.

Why wellness tips aren't enough

Breathing exercises help people cope. They don't change a caseload. When a team only gets tips, people hear that the problem is theirs.

The reliable person problem

Extra work flows to whoever handles it best. Over time, the team's strongest people carry the most and burn out first.

Fairness is visible

People notice who gets the hard cases, who gets flexibility and who gets thanked. Unfair loads hurt even people who aren't carrying them.

Practice: a hard case and a reliable colleague
A difficult new case comes in. The case manager always handles these well. What does the supervisor do?
A. Gives it to the case manager.
B. Checks the tracker and offers it to the person with the most room, with the case manager available to advise.
C. Takes it on themselves.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Making workload visible

Put the work where everyone can see it: a shared tracker, a weekly count or a quick round at the start of a huddle. You can't balance what you can't see.

The workload conversation

Ask what's on their plate, what's hardest and what could move. Decide one change together, and say when you'll check back.

What you can and can't change

You may not control staffing. You can control what gets dropped, delayed or shared, and you can make the case upward with numbers.

Practice: "just a busy season"
In a one-on-one, the case manager says, "I'm fine, it's just a busy season." The supervisor has seen the late emails. What do they say?
A. "Okay, let me know if that changes."
B. "I've noticed you're working late a lot. What's one thing we could take off your plate this month?"
C. "You need to take better care of yourself."
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Team practices that protect recovery

A rotation for the hardest cases. A no-meeting block each week. Coverage plans so time off is real time off.

Recognition that lands

Specific thanks, given soon, for the work and its effect on someone. "Your call got a family housed before winter" lands better than "great job."

Practice: reporting upward
The program manager asks the supervisor how their team is doing. What does the supervisor say?
A. "We're managing."
B. "Caseloads are up 30 percent and two people are out. I need one of two things from you."
C. Sends the program manager a long email listing every problem.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Making the case upward

Bring the trend, the risk and a request. "Caseloads are up 30 percent since spring. We're at risk of losing staff. I need one temporary position or permission to pause two programs."

What this is not

This isn't about lowering expectations or promising things you can't deliver. It is about being honest about capacity and acting on it.

Rewrite activity

Rewrite this team message so it is honest about the load and names a change: "I know everyone's busy. Let's push through until things settle down."

Your team's next step

At your next huddle, make the team's workload visible for five minutes, then decide one thing to share, delay or drop.

Shared culture, real responsibilities

Everyone can speak up about load. Supervisors assign the work and managers set staffing, so they carry most of the power to prevent burnout.

Reflection

Who on your team carries more than their share, and do they know you've noticed?

Closing

Teams don't burn out one person at a time. They burn out the way the work is set up, and that can be changed.

practice.title: Practice: a hard case and a reliable colleague
practice.question: A difficult new case comes in. The case manager always handles these well. What does the supervisor do?

options.text: Gives it to the case manager.
options.feedback: The case gets handled, and the case manager's load grows again. The pattern continues.

options.text: Checks the tracker and offers it to the person with the most room, with the case manager available to advise.
options.feedback: This spreads the load and still uses the case manager's skill without making it the case manager's case.

options.text: Takes it on themselves.
options.feedback: Generous, and it pulls the supervisor away from the supervising the team needs.

practice.title: Practice: "just a busy season"
practice.question: In a one-on-one, the case manager says, "I'm fine, it's just a busy season." The supervisor has seen the late emails. What do they say?

options.text: "Okay, let me know if that changes."
options.feedback: It respects the case manager's answer and leaves the real issue untouched.

options.text: "I've noticed you're working late a lot. What's one thing we could take off your plate this month?"
options.feedback: It names what the supervisor has seen, without judgment, and turns the talk toward a change.

options.text: "You need to take better care of yourself."
options.feedback: Kind in intent, and it puts the problem back on the case manager.

practice.title: Practice: reporting upward
practice.question: The program manager asks the supervisor how their team is doing. What does the supervisor say?

options.text: "We're managing."
options.feedback: It protects the team's image and hides the risk from the person who can help.

options.text: "Caseloads are up 30 percent and two people are out. I need one of two things from you."
options.feedback: Clear facts and a specific ask give the program manager something to act on.

options.text: Sends the program manager a long email listing every problem.
options.feedback: Honest, and hard to act on without a clear request.

title: Trauma-Informed Practice for Teams and Leaders
outcomes: Explain the six principles of a trauma-informed approach in plain terms.
Review one process or space through those principles.
Put in place one practice that supports staff exposed to secondary trauma.
summary: Many of the people we serve, and many of our own staff, carry the effects of trauma. This course helps leaders apply the six principles of a trauma-informed approach to how their division runs, and to support staff who are exposed to others' trauma every day.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Trauma-Informed Practice for Teams and Leaders
Leading with safety, trust and choice
Advanced self-directed learning

Opening case

A family arrives for an eligibility interview. The waiting room is loud, the security check is abrupt and the first question is about past evictions. The parent leaves before the interview starts. Down the hall, a case manager who handled a child protection call that morning is back at a desk with no break.

What trauma-informed means

A trauma-informed organization understands how common trauma is, recognizes its signs, builds that knowledge into how it works and tries not to cause harm again. It doesn't require knowing anyone's history.

Why it matters for leaders

Policies, spaces and schedules can calm people or put them on alert. Leaders decide most of those things.

Principle 1, safety

People need to feel physically and emotionally safe, in the lobby, on the phone and in team meetings.

Principle 2, trustworthiness and transparency

Say what will happen, why and what comes next. Keep the promises you make.

Principle 3, peer support

People with lived experience, and colleagues who have been through the same work, help others feel understood.

Principles 4 and 5, collaboration and choice

Share power where you can. Offer real choices, even small ones, and ask people what they need.

Principle 6, culture, history and gender

Trauma is shaped by racism, ableism, colonization and other harms that systems, ours included, have caused. Name that history and design with it in mind.

Practice: a lobby that feels unsafe
The county partner tells the program manager that families describe the lobby as "like a police station." What does the program manager do?
A. Explains that the security setup is required.
B. Walks through the lobby with the county partner and two parents, and asks what would help them feel safer.
C. Orders new lobby furniture.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Reviewing a process through the principles

Walk through a client's first visit step by step. At each step, ask: Is it safe? Is it clear? Is there a choice?

Secondary traumatic stress

Staff who hear about trauma every day can be affected by it. Signs include intrusive thoughts, avoidance and feeling on edge. It is a known result of the work, not a weakness.

Supporting exposed staff

Debrief after hard calls. Give people time between intense cases. Make sure supervision includes how people are doing, not only what they did.

Practice: after a fatality review
The supervisor's team handled a child fatality review this week. What does the program manager do?
A. Sends a thank-you email.
B. Offers a facilitated debrief, lighter assignments for a few days and a reminder about the Employee Assistance Program.
C. Asks the supervisor to check that everyone is okay.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Trauma-informed leadership in meetings

Share agendas ahead of time. Warn people before discussing hard material. Let people step out without explaining.

Practice: opening a hard discussion
A leadership meeting will cover a staff assault that happened last month. How does the program manager open?
A. Goes straight to the details.
B. Says what will be discussed, why, and that anyone can step out without explaining.
C. Skips the topic to avoid upsetting anyone.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

What this is not

This isn't therapy, and leaders aren't asked to diagnose anyone. It is a way to set up work so it does less harm.

Rewrite activity

Rewrite this appointment letter so it is clear, calm and offers a choice: "You must appear at the office on the date below. Failure to appear will result in case closure."

Your division's next step

Pick one client process or staff routine and review it through the six principles with the people who use it.

Shared culture, real responsibilities

Everyone can treat people with care. Leaders control spaces, policies and schedules, so a trauma-informed division depends most on their choices.

Reflection

Where in your division might a person feel least safe, and what would change that?

Closing

People can't take in help while they feel threatened. Safety comes first, for the people we serve and for the people who serve them.

practice.title: Practice: a lobby that feels unsafe
practice.question: The county partner tells the program manager that families describe the lobby as "like a police station." What does the program manager do?

options.text: Explains that the security setup is required.
options.feedback: It may be required, and the explanation leaves families' experience unchanged.

options.text: Walks through the lobby with the county partner and two parents, and asks what would help them feel safer.
options.feedback: This uses collaboration and choice, and finds changes that can work within security rules.

options.text: Orders new lobby furniture.
options.feedback: It may help, and it skips asking the people affected what matters most.

practice.title: Practice: after a fatality review
practice.question: The supervisor's team handled a child fatality review this week. What does the program manager do?

options.text: Sends a thank-you email.
options.feedback: Thanks matter, and an email alone may not reach what people are carrying.

options.text: Offers a facilitated debrief, lighter assignments for a few days and a reminder about the Employee Assistance Program.
options.feedback: This treats the effect of the work as real and gives people choices about support.

options.text: Asks the supervisor to check that everyone is okay.
options.feedback: Delegating care is reasonable, and the supervisor was exposed too.

practice.title: Practice: opening a hard discussion
practice.question: A leadership meeting will cover a staff assault that happened last month. How does the program manager open?

options.text: Goes straight to the details.
options.feedback: Efficient, and it can catch people off guard.

options.text: Says what will be discussed, why, and that anyone can step out without explaining.
options.feedback: Transparency and choice let people take part without being overwhelmed.

options.text: Skips the topic to avoid upsetting anyone.
options.feedback: Avoidance leaves people without answers and the safety issue unaddressed.
